items.q: Why does the scheduler scan an indexed next_run_at column instead of keeping an in-memory timer per job?

options.t: Timers are less precise than database scans
options.why: Backwards — an armed timer is actually more precise than a 1-second scan. Precision isn't the problem; durability and scale are.

options.t: Millions of armed timers vanish on every crash and must be rebuilt from the database anyway
options.why: Right. Millions of armed timers evaporate when the process dies, so you'd re-read the job store to re-arm them — at which point the durable, indexed scan IS your system, and the timers are decoration.

options.t: The database has no way to push a notification to the application at the exact moment a job's scheduled time arrives
options.why: Some can (LISTEN/NOTIFY, change streams), but that's not the reasoning. The scan wins because state survives crashes in the store and one index range read finds everything due.

options.t: Cron expressions are too complex to evaluate outside a database
options.why: Cron parsing happens in application code either way — we parse once at write time and materialize the next timestamp. The scan-vs-timers question is about durability and fleet-wide arbitration, not parsing.

items.q: In the claim query, what does SKIP LOCKED do?

options.t: It automatically retries rows that are locked by another transaction, using exponential backoff until each lock is released
options.why: No retrying happens at all — that's the beauty. Skipped rows are simply someone else's work; this scanner takes the next unlocked ones.

options.t: Prevents any other transaction from reading the table
options.why: That would be a table lock — a throughput disaster. Row-level locking plus skipping is precisely how many scanners work the same table concurrently.

options.t: Rows already locked by another transaction are silently passed over instead of waited on
options.why: Exactly. Combined with FOR UPDATE, each scanner grabs a disjoint batch of due rows: locked rows look invisible, so concurrent scanners partition the work without ever talking to each other.

options.t: Deletes rows whose locks have expired
options.why: Row locks don't expire on a timer and SKIP LOCKED deletes nothing. Locks vanish when their transaction commits or rolls back — that rollback is what un-claims a crashed scanner's rows.

items.q: A worker executes a job, then crashes before acknowledging. Why can't the scheduler know whether the work happened?

options.t: Because the worker writes its logs asynchronously, so the record proving the work finished may never have reached disk before the machine went down
options.why: Even perfect synchronous logging elsewhere doesn't help the coordinator decide in the moment — the fundamental issue is that the confirming message itself can always be the thing that's lost.

options.t: Silence looks the same whether the crash came just before or just after the work — the final ack can always be the lost message
options.why: That's the Two Generals problem in one sentence. No protocol fixes it: add more acks and the last ack is still the one that can vanish. Hence at-least-once or at-most-once — never exactly-once execution.

options.t: Because the database transaction was still open
options.why: The job's side effects (an API call, a sent email) usually live outside any scheduler transaction. Even with transactions, the ack-loss window exists for every external effect.

options.t: It can know, by checking the worker's exit code
options.why: A crashed or partitioned machine returns no exit code — that's the scenario. The absence of any signal is exactly the ambiguity.

items.q: What is the purpose of the lease (lease_expires_at) plus heartbeat on a running job?

options.t: To detect dead workers without killing long-running jobs — beats extend the lease; silence past expiry triggers reclaim
options.why: Right. The lease is a claim with a shelf life. A 6-hour job stays claimed through periodic renewals; a dead worker stops renewing and the reaper re-enqueues its run. Same idea as SQS visibility timeout.

options.t: To limit how long any job is allowed to run
options.why: That's the separate timeout_s config. The lease isn't a runtime cap — heartbeats can extend it indefinitely for legitimately long jobs.

options.t: To measure job duration for billing
options.why: Duration comes from started_at/finished_at on the run row. The lease exists for failure detection, not metering.

options.t: To prevent two users from editing the same job spec
options.why: Job-spec edits are ordinary row updates on the jobs table. Leases guard executions in the runs table — a different lifecycle entirely.

items.q: A 'misfire policy' decides:

options.t: How many times a job that failed with an error gets retried, and what backoff schedule separates the attempts
options.why: That's max_attempts with backoff. Misfire policy is about lateness — the scheduler being down when the job came due — not about the job failing.

options.t: What to do about firings that came due while the scheduler was down: run late, skip, or catch up
options.why: Correct. RUN_NOW fires once, late; SKIP waits for the next occurrence; CATCH_UP replays each missed occurrence. It's per-job config because no single answer fits both a daily digest and an hourly billing statement.

options.t: Which queue a job is dispatched to
options.why: That's the priority setting. Misfire policy only activates when firings are late.

options.t: Whether a job may run on multiple workers in parallel
options.why: Concurrency limits are a separate knob. Misfire is strictly about missed schedule times.

items.q: After a run exhausts max_attempts, the design moves it to a dead-letter state and alerts. Why alert instead of just storing it?

options.t: Because dead runs would otherwise sit in the queues, consuming capacity that live jobs will need during the next spike
options.why: Dead runs leave the queues entirely — capacity isn't the issue. The issue is that nobody looks at a graveyard unless something tells them to.

options.t: A DLQ nobody watches is a landfill — exhausted retries mean something is persistently broken and needs a human
options.why: Right. Retries-with-backoff already absorbed transient failures; what lands in the DLQ failed persistently. The arrival rate is a first-class alarm because a step change means some dependency broke for a whole class of jobs.

options.t: Regulations require notification of failed jobs
options.why: Compliance might apply to specific workloads, but the design rationale is operational: persistent failure demands attention regardless of regulation.

options.t: So the job can be automatically re-registered
options.why: Automatic resurrection would defeat max_attempts — you'd loop forever on a broken job. The DLQ is where automation stops and humans start.

items.q: Why is a job scheduler's load a 'heartbeat' rather than a smooth stream?

options.t: Databases batch their writes on second boundaries
options.why: DB write batching is internal and unrelated. The spikes come from what humans type into schedule fields, not from storage mechanics.

options.t: Humans schedule on round numbers — 0 * * * *, */5, and midnight — so firings pile up at minute, hour, and day boundaries
options.why: Exactly. Real crontab collections cluster brutally at round times; Google found it severe enough to add a '?' syntax so the system could smear the midnight mob. The wave, not the average, sizes your design.

options.t: Retries synchronize jobs into waves
options.why: Un-jittered retries can create waves (that's why backoff gets jitter), but the dominant, predictable spikes exist even with zero failures — they're baked into the schedules themselves.

options.t: The scanner tier only wakes once per hour
options.why: Scanners sweep every second. The load shape comes from when jobs are due, not from how often we look.

items.q: The cookbook says to key a job's side effects by (job_id, scheduled_for). Why not include the attempt number?

options.t: Attempt numbers are not stored anywhere
options.why: They are — the runs table tracks attempt. They're deliberately excluded from the key, not unavailable.

options.t: All executions of one firing must share a key so they collapse into one effect; per-attempt keys would defeat the dedup
options.why: Right. The key's job is to make every execution of the same logical firing hit the same guard. Include the attempt and attempt 2's charge sails past attempt 1's record — the exact double-charge you built the key to stop.

options.t: Including more fields makes the key too long for most databases
options.why: Key length is a non-issue — hash it if you care. The design question is which executions should collide, and the answer is: all executions of one scheduled firing.

options.t: Because scheduled_for is rewritten on every retry, the key already distinguishes attempts, so adding the attempt number on top would be redundant
options.why: Other way around: scheduled_for stays fixed across retries of the same firing — that stability is exactly what makes it the right key component.

items.q: Why is the runs row inserted inside the same transaction that claims the job and advances next_run_at?

options.t: It saves a database round trip
options.why: Round trips are a nice-to-have; the reason is correctness. Split the insert from the claim and there's a crash window where the job is marked fired but no record of the firing exists anywhere.

options.t: It lets the worker find its payload faster
options.why: Workers get the run_id from the queue and read the row either way. Transaction membership doesn't change read speed — it changes what crashes can lose.

options.t: The row is an outbox: if the scanner crashes after commit but before enqueueing, a sweeper finds the pending run and re-enqueues it — the firing can be delayed but never silently lost
options.why: Exactly. Advancing next_run_at means 'this occurrence is handled,' so the same commit must durably record the occurrence. The pending run row is the recoverable proof, and the sweeper is its safety net.

options.t: Postgres requires inserts and updates to share a transaction
options.why: No such requirement — you can split them freely. We choose not to, because atomicity between 'occurrence claimed' and 'occurrence recorded' is the whole guarantee.

items.q: A teammate's prototype has each scanner run SELECT ... WHERE next_run_at <= now() with no locking, then fire what it finds. With three scanners, what happens and what's the fix?

options.t: Roughly every due job fires three times; fix by making the read-and-claim atomic — FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, advancing next_run_at in the same transaction
options.why: Right. All three scanners see the same due rows in the same tick and all dispatch them. The claim must be an atomic arbitrated act; plain SELECTs don't arbitrate anything.

options.t: It mostly works in practice: the three scanners' ticks are offset by chance, so whichever scanner runs first advances next_run_at and the other two find nothing left due
options.why: Timing offsets shrink the race window; they don't close it. A correctness property that depends on scanners staying luckily out of phase is a duplicate-charge incident on a countdown.

options.t: Jobs fire once but in the wrong order; fix with ORDER BY
options.why: Ordering isn't the issue — multiplicity is. Each scanner independently fires the full due set; ORDER BY just makes them duplicate in the same sequence.

options.t: The database deadlocks; fix by using one scanner
options.why: Plain SELECTs take no conflicting locks, so no deadlock — it 'works' while triple-firing, which is worse. Dropping to one scanner trades the bug for a SPOF; the row-claim fix keeps both correctness and redundancy.

items.q: A billing job charged a card, then its worker died before acking. The reaper re-enqueued the run and a second worker executed it. The customer was charged once. Which mechanism most likely deserves the credit?

options.t: The queue deduplicated the second delivery
options.why: The second delivery wasn't a queue duplicate — the reaper legitimately re-enqueued after lease expiry. The queue did its job by delivering; the guard has to live in the job's effects.

options.t: A conditional write keyed on the firing — e.g. set invoice to 'paid' where still 'due', or the payment provider deduping on an idempotency key
options.why: Right. The re-run executed fully — at-least-once promises nothing less. It reached the side effect, found the (job_id, scheduled_for) guard already tripped, and became a no-op. This is the cookbook working as designed.

options.t: The lease prevented the second worker from starting
options.why: The lease had already expired — that's precisely why the re-run happened. Leases make duplicates rare; they cannot make them impossible.

options.t: The scheduler detected the first execution succeeded
options.why: It structurally couldn't — the ack never arrived, and silence is ambiguous (Two Generals). If the scheduler could detect success through silence, none of this machinery would exist.

items.q: A 6-hour ML training job keeps getting killed and restarted by the scheduler every couple of minutes. Most likely cause?

options.t: The job's worker isn't heartbeating, so its 90-second lease expires mid-run and the reaper reclaims a healthy run
options.why: Classic. The lease default assumes periodic renewal; a worker that claims and goes silent for 6 hours looks exactly like a dead worker at minute two. Fix: heartbeat every 30s (extending the lease), and alert on reclaims of heartbeat-capable jobs.

options.t: Someone edited the job's cron expression to every-two-minutes, so the scheduler is dutifully launching a brand-new training run each time it comes due
options.why: Possible in theory, but the symptom is restarts of the same run (attempt incrementing), not new scheduled firings — the runs table distinguishes these at a glance.

options.t: The DLQ is re-injecting the job
options.why: DLQ is where runs stop, not a re-injection path — automatic resurrection would defeat max_attempts entirely.

options.t: SKIP LOCKED is skipping the job's row
options.why: SKIP LOCKED affects which scanner claims a due job; this job was claimed and started fine. The problem is downstream, in the run's lease lifecycle.

items.q: Your fire-time-skew p99 alarm trips every midnight UTC as hundreds of thousands of daily jobs come due at once. The sustainable response is:

options.t: Provision the claim path and queue brokers for the peak second — scale the database until the entire midnight wave can dispatch inside the SLO
options.why: You'd be provisioning the whole system for one second of the day, and the wave grows with job count forever. The claim path isn't even the slow part — worker drain time is.

options.t: Move the scan tick from 1 second to 100 ms
options.why: Scanning faster finds the same 300K due jobs at the same instant. The wave exists in the schedule data; scan frequency doesn't touch it.

options.t: Smear the wave: jitter for jobs that opt into flexible timing (Google's '?' idea), autoscale bulk workers ahead of the spike, and set per-tier SLOs
options.why: Right — attack the cause (schedule clustering) where jobs permit, add elastic capacity for the residue, and stop paging on bulk work meeting a bulk SLO. Most midnight jobs don't actually need second-zero execution; the API should make that expressible.

options.t: Drop firings that exceed the SLO
options.why: That converts a latency miss into silent data loss — the one failure the requirements made non-negotiable. Late is a policy question; lost is a broken promise.

items.q: The scheduler was down 09:00–09:12. Job A generates hourly billing statements (payload parameterized by the hour). Job B refreshes a cache every 5 minutes. The right misfire policies:

options.t: A: CATCH_UP — each missed hour must produce its statement. B: SKIP — a stale refresh is worthless with the next one minutes away
options.why: Right, and note why they differ: A's output is per-occurrence, so occurrences are irreplaceable; B's runs are interchangeable, so only the next one matters. Misfire policy is a property of the job's semantics — which is why it's per-job config.

options.t: Both CATCH_UP — after any outage, replaying every missed occurrence is the only policy that provably loses nothing, whatever the job happens to do
options.why: Catching up B replays a pile of identical stale refreshes — pointless load, and after a longer outage it's a self-inflicted thundering herd. 'Safe' defaults that replay everything are how outages get a second act.

options.t: Both SKIP, to avoid surprise load after recovery
options.why: Skipping A silently drops the 09:00 statement — a data hole someone finds during an audit. Load caution is right for B and wrong for A; one policy can't serve both.

options.t: Both RUN_NOW
options.why: A fires once at 09:12 — but if the outage had spanned two occurrences, one statement vanishes; CATCH_UP is what guarantees per-occurrence output. B running at 09:12 is harmless but pointless with a 09:15 refresh seconds behind it.

items.q: Certificate-rotation jobs (critical, rare) are sitting behind 200K thumbnail re-encodes (bulk). You have one queue and one worker pool. Best fix?

options.t: Separate queues per priority tier with dedicated worker pools, so critical always has reserved capacity
options.why: Right. Dedicated pools give each tier a capacity floor — bulk backlogs can't touch critical's workers, and bulk still makes progress. The cost, some idle reserved capacity, is cheap insurance against an expired certificate.

options.t: One queue where workers always take the highest-priority item first
options.why: Strict priority fixes today's symptom and creates tomorrow's: sustained critical traffic starves bulk forever, and 'forever' eventually includes something that mattered. Starvation guards beat strict ordering.

options.t: Have critical jobs bypass the queue and run on the scanner nodes
options.why: Now scanner health depends on arbitrary job payloads — a memory-hungry rotation job can take down the firing tier. Keep deciding and executing separated; that separation is why the Slack cron box had to die.

options.t: Raise max_attempts on critical jobs so they eventually get through
options.why: Retries address failure; this is starvation — the jobs aren't failing, they're waiting. More attempts just means more patient waiting behind the same 200K thumbnails.

items.q: A scanner commits its claim transaction, then crashes before enqueueing the 500 run_ids. What happens to those firings?

options.t: They're lost — next_run_at already advanced, so nothing will refire them
options.why: That would be true without the outbox — which is why the run rows exist. The pending rows survive the crash in the database; the design closed exactly this window.

options.t: The sweeper finds runs stuck in 'pending', re-enqueues them minutes late, and the workers' conditional claim makes any double-enqueue harmless
options.why: Right — this is the outbox pattern earning its keep. Delayed, never lost. And if some runs were actually enqueued before the crash, the conditional state='pending' claim means a second delivery finds a non-pending run and drops dead.

options.t: The transaction rolls back automatically since enqueueing never happened
options.why: The commit already happened — the database can't know an application-level enqueue was still owed. Rollback saves you when the crash is mid-transaction; after commit, recovery needs the sweeper.

options.t: Nothing is lost: the next one-second scan tick simply sees the same 500 jobs still sitting due in the index and re-claims the whole batch itself
options.why: It can't — next_run_at moved to each job's next occurrence, so those jobs aren't due anymore. Recovery has to come from the runs table, not the jobs table.

items.q: build_ledger must run after pull_orders, pull_refunds, and pull_fx_rates all succeed. Two parents finish in the same millisecond. What makes build_ledger fire exactly once?

options.t: Each completion does an atomic conditional decrement of the child's unmet-dependency counter in the database; only the update that lands on zero triggers the child
options.why: Right. Atomicity pushes the race into the database, where one decrement serializes after the other — exactly one observes the transition to zero. Fan-in is 'counter hits zero exactly once,' and that's a conditional-write problem.

options.t: Each parent's handler reads the counter, and whoever reads zero fires the child
options.why: Read-then-write is the race: both handlers read 1 simultaneously, both decrement, and either both fire the child (duplicate) or each thinks the other will (never fires). This is the exact bug conditional writes exist to kill.

options.t: Parents are forced to run sequentially so completions can't collide
options.why: Works, but you just serialized a fan-in whose entire point is parallel extracts — tripling the pipeline's wall-clock time to dodge a one-line atomic update is the wrong trade.

options.t: The child subscribes to the queue and fires on the third completion event it sees
options.why: At-least-once delivery means completion events can arrive duplicated — count events naively and a redelivered event looks like a third parent. The dedup you'd need to add is the counter table you were avoiding.

items.q: A scanner node's clock is 40 seconds fast. In the SKIP LOCKED design, what goes wrong with firing correctness?

options.t: Every job that scanner claims fires 40 seconds ahead of schedule, and precision-sensitive jobs quietly miss their windows
options.why: It would, if the claim compared against the scanner's clock. It doesn't — now() in the claim query evaluates on the database server. The scanner's clock never enters the due-ness decision.

options.t: Nothing — due-ness is decided by now() on the database's clock, one authoritative clock for every scanner
options.why: Right, and it's an underrated virtue of DB-arbitrated claiming. Contrast Quartz clustering, where nodes use their own clocks and the docs demand NTP sync within a second or you get missed and duplicated firings.

options.t: Its claims deadlock against correctly-clocked scanners
options.why: Lock behavior has nothing to do with wall clocks — SKIP LOCKED scanners never wait on each other, whatever their clocks say.

options.t: It double-fires jobs claimed by other scanners
options.why: Double-firing is prevented by row locks, which are clock-independent. A locked row is skipped whether your clock is fast, slow, or right.

items.q: The interviewer asks: 'Row-claiming through the database, or a leader-elected scheduler tier?' The strongest senior answer:

options.t: "SKIP LOCKED row claims. The store must arbitrate firings anyway — even a leader needs fencing enforced there — so I skip the election, get crash recovery from transaction rollback, and scale scanners freely. Ceiling: a few thousand claims/sec on one store; past that I shard the claim path. Leader election wins if firing needs rich in-memory state."
options.why: A commitment, the load-bearing reason (the arbiter exists either way), a named ceiling with its escape route, and the honest case for the road not taken. This is the full E5 shape — and it's also what Airflow 2.0 actually ships.

options.t: "Leader election with etcd. One active firer eliminates the claim race by construction, followers give me hot standby, and it's the pattern Google's own cron uses — proven at the largest scale there is."
options.why: Fluent, but it borrows Google's authority instead of engaging this design: the failover gap, the single-leader midnight ceiling — and a leader without fencing at the store still double-fires after a GC pause. The hard part didn't go away; it got a second component in front of it.

options.t: "Both are valid; it depends on the team's operational comfort."
options.why: True and empty — the option-listing hedge that caps candidates at mid-level. The interviewer asked for a decision; comfort matters in real life, but the merits here are arguable and you were asked to argue them.

options.t: "Neither — use a distributed lock in Redis per job."
options.why: A per-job Redis lock re-implements row claiming with weaker guarantees: no transactional tie between 'lock held' and 'next_run_at advanced', and lock expiry during a slow claim reopens the double-fire race. You'd rebuild fencing by hand to fix it.

items.q: Interviewer: 'Can you guarantee each job executes exactly once?' The senior answer:

options.t: "Yes — with a dedup table checked before every execution."
options.why: The check-then-execute gap is the hole: crash after the external side effect but before recording it, and the re-run's check passes. A dedup table moves the guarantee closer; it cannot close the window around effects it doesn't transactionally own.

options.t: "Yes, if we use Kafka's exactly-once semantics for dispatch."
options.why: Kafka's EOS covers consume-process-produce loops whose effects stay inside Kafka transactions. A job that calls a payment API leaves that world immediately — the guarantee doesn't travel.

options.t: "No. An arbiter makes firing exactly-once-ish, but execution can't be — a worker's silence hides whether the work happened (Two Generals). So: at-least-once, plus an idempotency contract."
options.why: The honest no, the reason it's a no, and the committed engineering answer to living with it. Saying 'no' crisply here is one of the strongest signals this problem can elicit — it's the sentence the whole question exists to fish for.

options.t: "Effectively yes. With conditional claims, heartbeat leases, and a reaper, a duplicate needs a crash inside a millisecond-wide window — at our volumes that is rare enough to treat as never."
options.why: 'Rare' times millions of firings a day is 'weekly incident.' Leases shrink the duplicate rate; only idempotency makes duplicates harmless. Rounding rare to never is how double-charges reach production.

items.q: At 10x (100M jobs, ~17K firings/sec), what saturates first, and what's the fix that preserves the design?

options.t: The queue brokers — switch to a faster message bus
options.why: 17K msgs/sec is a light morning for Kafka or SQS — orders of magnitude of headroom remain. Naming the queue here suggests guessing rather than tracing the load to where coordination actually concentrates.

options.t: The claim path: tens of thousands of contended row locks/sec on one store's index range. Hash-partition jobs into shards, scanners sweep disjoint shards — claims stop contending and the design multiplies instead of reshaping
options.why: Right. The arbiter is where all coordination funnels, so it's where 10x lands. Sharding the claim keeps every property — transactional claims, rollback recovery, outbox — per shard. Knowing which bottleneck arrives first, and that the fix is multiplication not redesign, is the senior read.

options.t: The cron parser — 100M expressions is too many to evaluate
options.why: Expressions are parsed once at registration and materialized into next_run_at; the hot path never parses cron. That's precisely why the materialized column exists.

options.t: Everything at once — the design needs a rewrite on dynamo-style storage
options.why: Load doesn't hit uniformly; it concentrates at the coordination point. 'Rewrite everything' skips the diagnosis, discards working transactional machinery, and would rebuild claims on a store without the row locks that made them simple.

items.q: You have 20 minutes of deep-dive time for the scheduler. Where do you spend it?

options.t: The claim protocol and duplicate-execution semantics — the atomic fire arbitration, crash windows, leases, and the idempotency contract
options.why: That's the fire this question was invented to probe: every catastrophic failure mode (zero fires, two fires) lives there, and it's where distributed-systems judgment shows. Everything else in this design is assembled from parts any senior knows.

options.t: Cron expression parsing and timezone handling
options.why: Real work, zero design tension — it's a library call plus materialization at write time. Twenty minutes here is touring the curtains while the claim race burns.

options.t: The dispatch layer: comparing Kafka, SQS, and RabbitMQ on delivery guarantees, ordering, throughput ceilings, and operational cost to justify the broker choice
options.why: At 1,700 msgs/sec any of them yawns. Broker comparison is a blog post, not a crux — and the interviewer hears 'buzzword comfort zone' when candidates settle there.

options.t: The REST API design and pagination of run history
options.why: Necessary, quick, and unremarkable — the API section's job is to get out of the way. No senior signal lives in pagination.

items.q: Which alert catches 'the scheduler silently stopped firing anything' — and why do the others miss it?

options.t: Error rate on the scanner tier
options.why: A wedged scanner emits no errors — it emits nothing. When the failure is absence of action, error-rate alarms are structurally blind; there are no failed requests because there are no requests.

options.t: DLQ arrival rate
options.why: The DLQ fills when jobs run and fail. Nothing running means a DLQ flatlining at zero — which looks identical to a perfectly healthy day.

options.t: Worker CPU utilization dropping
options.why: It does drop — along with every other metric, ambiguously. Low CPU also means a quiet Sunday. You'd be inferring the outage from a shadow instead of measuring the thing itself.

options.t: An 'oldest unclaimed due job' gauge that climbs when firing stops, plus a dead-man's-switch canary whose absence pages via an external monitor
options.why: Right — alert on the absence of expected events, with one watcher outside the system's own blast radius. The gauge measures 'firing has stopped' directly; the external canary survives even the database or metrics pipeline dying with the scanners.

items.q: You're shipping a rewritten cron-parsing library to the scheduler. The senior rollout:

options.t: Deploy to one scanner first and watch error rates
options.why: A parser bug doesn't error — it happily computes a wrong next_run_at and corrupts schedules for every job that canary touches. Canarying catches crashes; it's blind to silent wrongness, which is this change's actual risk.

options.t: Shadow mode: new parser computes next occurrences alongside the old for days of real schedules, diff the outputs, ship only at zero diffs — because the failure mode is silent corruption of next_run_at, not crashes
options.why: Right. Name the failure mode first, then pick the rollout that can see it. Diffing shadow computations turns 'millions of jobs silently drift to wrong times' into a boring report before any production write happens.

options.t: Ship behind a feature flag and flip it globally after a week of soak
options.why: The flag gives you fast rollback of the code, but not of the data: wrong next_run_at values written during the soak stay wrong after the flip back. Reversible deploy, irreversible corruption.

options.t: Rely on the test suite — cron parsing is pure logic with full coverage
options.why: Tests cover the expressions you thought of; 10M users have submitted the ones you didn't. Shadow-diffing against production's actual expressions is the test suite reality writes for you.

items.q: Suppose you had chosen the leader-elected variant. The leader stalls in a 90-second GC pause, its etcd lease expires, a new leader takes over — then the old one wakes and fires its pending batch. What actually prevents duplicates?

options.t: Nothing needed — etcd guarantees only one leader exists
options.why: etcd guarantees at most one valid lease, but the stale leader doesn't know it's stale — it was unconscious when the lease lapsed. Between waking and checking, it acts. Election limits who should act; it can't stop a zombie that already thinks it may.

options.t: A fencing token: each term carries a monotonically increasing number, and the job store rejects claim writes bearing a stale term
options.why: Right, the chapter 2.3 payoff. The fence must live at the point of write, in the store — which is the quiet argument for the SKIP LOCKED design: if the store must be the bouncer anyway, let it run the whole door.

options.t: Size the lease so no realistic GC pause can outlast it — say ten minutes — so a stalled leader always wakes up still holding a valid lease
options.why: Now failover takes minutes every time a leader genuinely dies, and the next pathological pause — a network partition, a VM migration — outlasts the new number anyway. Tuning timeouts against unbounded delays is a race you lose on schedule.

options.t: The old leader checks its lease immediately before firing
options.why: Check-then-fire has a gap: the lease can expire between the check and the fire — a GC pause can land exactly there, and this scenario proves it happens. Validity must be verified atomically with the write, which is what a fencing token does.
